abstract: Camelina sativa is an emerging oilseed crop for low-input and climate-resilient agriculture, valued for its agronomic versatility and tolerance to abiotic stress. However, how drought affects its seeds, and whether these effects carry over to the next generation, remains poorly understood. We grew six Camelina accessions at 100% (control) and 20% (drought) soil water content and followed their responses from vegetative growth to seed mucilage content and germination. Drought reduced stomatal conductance and increased leaf temperature in all accessions, whereas its effect on shoot growth changed over time and differed among accessions. Drought-stressed plants developed a more compact shoot, with shorter secondary stems, inflorescences and internodes and 43% higher secondary stem density. Seed yield per plant fell by 47%, but seeds were 38% heavier and 28% larger in all accessions, consistent with plants prioritizing the provisioning of individual seeds over seed number. These larger seeds had a 27% smaller mucilage area relative to their size, suggesting that drought shifts maternal allocation away from the seed coat, which could affect seedling establishment. Drought also shifted the monosaccharide composition of seed mucilage, mainly in the non-adherent fraction, where rhamnose increased and galactose decreased in only one accession (CAM230), whereas in the adherent fraction it lowered the proportion of galacturonic acid. Despite their larger size, progeny of drought-stressed plants germinated less under salt (NaCl) and osmotic (PEG) stress, and under PEG (-0.6 MPa) germination fell by up to 26 percentage points in half of the accessions. These results reflect differences among accessions in how shoot growth responds to drought over time and a cost of maternal drought for the progeny. Both should be considered when selecting Camelina for drought-prone, low-input systems.
